strengths: Addresses genuine gap in benchmarking fine-grained visual reasoning with structured diagrams, particularly high-resolution transit maps
Comprehensive dataset with careful construction: 1,008 QA pairs from 30 cities in 13 countries with multilingual support and manual verification
Well-designed two-level evaluation framework measuring both correctness and quality, with difficulty-aware weighting scheme
Extensive evaluation of 15 diverse MLLMs with both base and reasoning variants, revealing counterintuitive findings about model performance patterns
Strong evidence that fine-grained spatial reasoning requires genuine visual perception, demonstrated through ablation with masked visual input
Excellent reproducibility: detailed pipeline documentation, map sources, experimental setup, and planned code release
Comprehensive error analysis categorizing failure modes (visual confusion, format errors, hallucination, refusal)
weaknesses: Test set limited to 312 samples, reducing statistical significance relative to recent benchmarks (e.g., MMMU with 11.5k samples)
Most significant finding (base models outperforming reasoning models in open-source) lacks rigorous investigation and appears speculative in its explanations
Evaluation metric design choices appear ad-hoc: map score components (point allocations like 2 for route name) lack justification or ablation studies, and no inter-annotator agreement reported
Limited scope: single task type (route planning), only 4 languages, 30 cities; generalization to other spatial reasoning tasks and geographic/linguistic contexts unclear
Dataset validation incomplete: MLLM-assisted extraction error rates not reported, optimal route definition not explained when multiple valid routes exist, inter-annotator agreement absent
No analysis of which specific visual features cause model failures (line colors, station complexity, branching topology) or why performance varies significantly across cities with similar difficulty
Text-only ablation is artificial since models aren't trained for text-only visual tasks; no few-shot or fine-tuning experiments to understand learning capacity
Quality evaluation algorithm appears simplistic with unexplained design choices (e.g., adding 10-point bonus for correct answers in quality score); no sensitivity analysis on scoring parameters

strengths: Well-motivated benchmark design using transit maps to evaluate fine-grained visual reasoning without external tool shortcuts

Comprehensive and carefully constructed dataset with high-resolution images (5,839 × 5,449 pixels), geographic diversity (30 cities, 13 countries), multilingual support, and quality control procedures
Thorough experimental evaluation across 15 MLLMs with rich analysis (difficulty breakdowns, city-level variation, error categorization, visual input ablation)
Interesting counterintuitive finding that open-source base models outperform reasoning variants while closed-source shows opposite pattern
Clear presentation with informative visualizations and comprehensive appendix
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale: only 312 test samples across 11 cities; small by benchmark standards and limits confidence in findings. Questions are highly formulaic with only 2 types and 3 templates, requiring strict format compliance rather than testing diverse reasoning

Evaluation metrics lack rigorous justification: map score is ad-hoc with arbitrary point allocations and capping values; difficulty weighting (1.0-3.0) unexplained; no human validation, inter-rater agreement, or ablation studies on scoring choices

Main finding (open vs. closed-source reasoning pattern) is stated but not rigorously investigated—proposed explanation is speculative without controlled experiments or ablation studies to test the hypothesis

Narrow problem scope: essentially a lookup-and-ordering task limited to route planning between two stops; results specific to transit maps with unclear generalization to other fine-grained visual reasoning tasks acknowledged by authors

Significant experimental design gaps: test set selection procedure unclear, incomplete text-only evaluation (subset of models only), missing human baseline, no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals, different image handling strategies across models not adequately addressed for fair comparison

Technical concerns: algorithms 1 & 2 contribute no methodological novelty; response invalidation handling not analyzed; text-only results show anomalies (some models improve without visual input) that contradict main thesis and aren't investigated
Limited error analysis depth: qualitative breakdown in Figure 5 lacks quantitative categorization by error type, correlation with model properties, or systematic patterns across difficulty levels

Insufficient justification for design choices: why specific cap values for map score? Why average IoU and exact match? How are route conflicts between map services resolved? These lack principled explanation

strengths: Addresses meaningful gap: Fine-grained visual reasoning on structured, information-dense diagrams (transit maps) is underexplored despite its practical relevance
High-resolution images (avg. 5,839×5,449 pixels) genuinely test fine-grained visual perception, substantially exceeding existing benchmarks
Well-designed semi-automated construction pipeline with three stages (collection, QA construction, quality control) is transparent, reproducible, and scalable
Novel two-level evaluation framework distinguishing correctness (accuracy) from quality (map score) based on route efficiency and alignment, providing nuanced assessment
Counterintuitive empirical finding: open-source reasoning models underperform base variants while closed-source shows opposite trend—surprising and actionable insight
Rigorous text-only ablation study demonstrates that genuine visual perception remains essential despite strong prior knowledge, validating task design
Comprehensive experiments: 15 diverse MLLMs, both open/closed-source, reasoning/base variants, across difficulty combinations and cities
Strong transparency and reproducibility: detailed algorithms, ethical considerations, planned code release under MIT License, multilingual support
weaknesses: Critically small test set (312 samples) with highly imbalanced difficulty buckets (e.g., 1 sample for hard-middle) prevents robust statistical conclusions; no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance estimates provided

Single-domain limitation severely constrains generalizability claims—findings on transit maps may not transfer to other structured diagrams (flowcharts, circuits, tables); paper acknowledges but doesn't address this fundamental limitation

Shallow analysis of core finding: explanation for reasoning model underperformance is speculative and incompletely validated on this dataset; reasoning token quality never systematically analyzed; per-model error breakdowns absent

Map score evaluation metric insufficiently validated: multiple hand-crafted components lack ablation studies; no inter-rater reliability study; no validation that metric correlates with practical utility
Reference route reliability questionable: ground truth relies on Gaode/Google Map APIs without validation that routes are correct or optimal; potential label noise undiscussed

Methodological fairness concerns in model comparison: open-source and closed-source models use different image processing strategies, token limits (2,048 vs. default), and optimization approaches; confounds may explain observed patterns

Question difficulty assignment oversimplified: using only transfer count (0=easy, 1=medium, ≥2=hard) is crude proxy; no validation that labeling correlates with actual difficulty; overlooking other complexity dimensions

Insufficient error quantification: Figure 5 provides examples but lacks systematic breakdown; percentage of visual confusion vs. format errors vs. hallucination vs. refusal not reported; no analysis of which map features cause failures
Generalization claims not validated: counterintuitive reasoning model finding hasn't been tested on other visual reasoning tasks; unclear if specific to transit maps or holds broadly
Dataset diversity limitations: hard questions severely underrepresented (7.8%); imbalanced city samples; only 3 question templates; template coverage of reasoning types not justified

strengths: Addresses a clear gap in existing benchmarks by focusing on fine-grained spatial reasoning with high-resolution transit maps, filling an important niche between symbolic reasoning and coarse visual understanding tasks
Rigorous and comprehensive dataset construction with semi-automated pipeline, dual quality control (automated + manual), and balanced difficulty distribution across 30 cities in 15 countries

Well-designed two-level evaluation framework with correctness verification (via detailed route algorithms) and quality assessment (map score), coupled with difficulty-aware weighting for fair comparison
Extensive benchmarking study of 16 diverse MLLMs with systematic evaluation revealing concrete performance gaps and limitations in spatial reasoning capabilities

Thorough error analysis with detailed categorization of failure modes (grounding errors, hallucinations, spatial reasoning failures) illustrated with concrete examples, providing actionable insights for future research
Strong reproducibility: clear algorithms (Algorithms 1-2), detailed implementation in appendices, question templates provided, commitment to public dataset release with supplementary code
Comprehensive supplementary experiments including text-only evaluation, RL baseline training, symbolic representation ablations, and validation on OCR Bench
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily a benchmark paper without novel algorithms, architectures, or evaluation metrics; GRPO-based RL baseline is borrowed directly from prior work
Modest dataset scale (1,008 QA pairs) compared to recent benchmarks (MathVQA: 2,612; MMMU: 2,604), with limited diversity from only 30 cities and predefined question templates
Shallow analysis of root causes of model failures; lacks investigation of which architectural components contribute to spatial reasoning deficits and how to actually improve performance

Evaluation metric limitations: binary route matching ignores near-misses; via-stop scoring capped at 10 creates information loss; no inter-annotator agreement or human performance baseline; map score assumes single ground truth despite multiple valid routes
Incomplete visual-linguistic analysis despite having text-only experiments; lacks breakdown of which reasoning components are visual-dependent or systematic ablation of needed visual information

No generalization analysis across unseen cities or countries; unclear whether models learn generalizable spatial reasoning or map-specific patterns; no evidence that improvements transfer to downstream applications
Limited architectural guidance: no systematic comparison of reasoning vs. base models, no model scaling analysis, no investigation of how existing spatial reasoning modules help
Potential dataset biases not addressed: geographic concentration (heavy Asia representation), language imbalance, no analysis of geographic or linguistic model biases

RL training baseline provides only modest improvements (2-3% gain in Table 4) with plateau around 60-70% accuracy on short questions, raising questions about task feasibility and whether realistic improvements are possible
Some design choices appear arbitrary (difficulty thresholds, template selection) and lack empirical justification; limited validation against human judgments

strengths: Well-motivated and important benchmark addressing fine-grained visual reasoning evaluation gap in MLLMs
Comprehensive and carefully-constructed dataset with semi-automated quality control pipeline and extensive manual verification
Thoughtful multi-level evaluation framework with two evaluation metrics (correctness and quality) and difficulty-aware weighting
Broad experimental coverage of 16 MLLMs across different categories with systematic ablations on visual input
Extensive supplementary materials with detailed templates, quality control procedures, error analysis, and case studies
Good documentation of dataset construction methodology with transparent procedures for question generation and annotation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—purely a dataset/benchmark paper without novel modeling methods or algorithmic contributions; GRPO-based RL baseline is standard application of existing techniques
Modest dataset scale (1,008 QA pairs) and limited geographic scope (30 cities from 13 countries) reduces statistical power and may introduce geographic/cultural biases
Arbitrary design choices in evaluation algorithms (Algorithm 1-2) lack principled justification: fixed thresholds, weight matrices, and bonus points are ad-hoc without empirical validation
Missing inter-rater agreement statistics (Cohen's Kappa, agreement percentages); quality control section mentions manual correction but provides no quantitative error rates or agreement metrics
Shallow analysis of results—error analysis identifies generic failure modes without deeper investigation; observation that reasoning models don't outperform base models is noted but unexplained
Incomplete experimental analysis: no systematic breakdown by question type or difficulty level across model families; missing baseline comparisons with classical vision or simpler approaches
Sparse details on RL training baseline (Section 4.3): unclear implementation details, missing convergence criteria, modest improvements (1-2%) without statistical significance testing

Limited insights into fundamental questions about spatial reasoning in MLLMs; no investigation of what makes transit map reasoning difficult (visual perception, spatial reasoning, or language understanding)
No validation that assigned difficulty labels empirically correlate with actual model performance; difficulty-aware weighting scheme not empirically justified

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: Provides the first comprehensive benchmark specifically designed for fine-grained visual reasoning in high-resolution spatial artifacts (transit maps), filling an important evaluation void for MLLMs.

Exemplary dataset construction: The semi-automated pipeline with multi-stage human verification, comprehensive quality control, and two-level difficulty labeling demonstrates meticulous curation across 30 cities and 15 countries.

Thorough experimental evaluation: Comprehensive assessment of 16 MLLMs with detailed ablations (with/without visual input), error analysis with failure categorization, RL-based training baseline, and systematic performance breakdowns across cities, languages, and difficulty levels.

Well-designed evaluation framework: Two-level evaluation separating correctness (accuracy) from quality (map score) with explicit algorithms and clear evaluation procedures; provides reproducible metrics for spatial reasoning assessment.

Strong presentation and documentation: Clear writing, informative visualizations, and extensive supplementary material with algorithms, templates, case studies, and detailed construction procedures supporting reproducibility.
Responsible research practices: Thoughtful discussion of ethics, licensing, public implementation plans, data privacy, and research integrity considerations appropriate for a benchmark contribution.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Primary contribution is dataset creation and evaluation framework rather than algorithmic innovation. Methods used (GRPO-based RL, standard MLLMs) are established techniques, limiting scientific novelty suitable for a top venue.

Modest dataset scale relative to contemporary benchmarks: 1,008 QA pairs is relatively small (contemporary benchmarks often exceed 100K examples); 30 cities across 15 countries provides limited geographic diversity for claims about generalization.

Evaluation metric design concerns: The map score involves multiple manually-weighted components; single ground-truth route assumption underestimates capability when multiple valid routes exist; quality assessment includes subjective decisions not fully justified.

Insufficient analysis of dramatic performance plateau: Best models achieve only 43-45% accuracy on short questions and 17-21% on long questions; paper doesn't adequately investigate whether this reflects benchmark over-difficulty, fundamental model limitations, or misalignment between benchmark design and capability assessment.

Incomplete failure mode analysis: While error categorization is provided, investigation remains surface-level regarding why models fundamentally fail at spatial reasoning, text localization, and structured output generation; misses opportunity to inform future model development.

Limited differentiation from related work: Could better distinguish from existing spatial reasoning benchmarks (CityBench, MapBench) and geospatial tasks; unclear what unique insights ReasonMap provides beyond the domain specificity.

Domain-specific limitations: Restriction to transit maps is narrow; unclear how insights generalize to broader spatial reasoning tasks or other structured visual artifacts (floor plans, technical diagrams, etc.).

Reproducibility gaps: Exact prompting strategies beyond appendix examples unclear; inter-rater agreement statistics for difficulty annotation missing; convergence analysis for training baseline incomplete.
